01 · The problem

Platforms are anything you have to log into.

Gardens, Not Platforms · Megan Ducote

5 companies
deliver news to 63% of the world. They replaced the town square and locked the doors.

2h 21m
per day, on average, doom scrolling. Feeds engineered to hold your attention, not serve your interests.

They did not build the town square. They captured it, and now they rent it back to you.

03 · The convenience trap

Anatomy of platform lock-in.

In exchange for control of your identity, your data, your relationships and your reach, platforms offer you this.

🔍
Discovery
The algorithm decided who saw what, and when.
✨
Ease of use
Free tier. No configuration. Where everyone already was.
🌐
Availability
Always on. Your data on their servers, reachable from any device.
All three required centralisation. Until now.
What do platforms give you?
  • Your data on their servers
  • Discovery by algorithm
  • Growth as the only metric
  • You are the product
What does a garden give you?
  • Your data on your device
  • Discovery by values
  • Sufficiency as the design goal
  • You are the gardener

06 · The three horizons

Citizen infrastructure is the transition.

Horizon one is what dominates now. Horizon three is what we are aiming at. The middle is the part most visions skip.

1 / 2

Horizon 1

Cultivate your data

You hold your own data and run your own models on it.

Horizon 2

Protect community intelligence

Work passes peer to peer, and a commons holds its shape between meetings.

Horizon 3

Enable emergent governance

Communities find each other by principle and activity, without re-centralising.

07 · The spec

The technology Houston Bloom runs on is a Community Legibility Spec.

Founder’s Couch, episode one · Megan Ducote

Authentication without a central authority. A community broadcasts an anonymised record of its activity; each participant keeps a private, append-only ledger. Authentication is the comparison of the two: you show your record overlaps the community broadcast, without the community ever naming you.

What a member contributes to the commons is a redacted manifest: an opaque identifier, a timestamp, and the design principle the work stands on. No names, no paths, no content. The work itself never moves.

Instead of giving you my ID attached to my email, what if I gave you the timestamps of what I shared at a networking event? I have my timestamps. The community has them too. It becomes proof of action, anonymised.

Published paper
Dual-Ledger Authentication
Membership proven by two records that overlap. No login, no identity provider, no issuing authority.
